children.text: Two weeks is not a length of time for seeing all of Egypt. It is a length of time for choosing what to see, managing the fatigue of moving between places, and reading the spine of the country along the line of the Nile.
When you have
two weeks
in Egypt, the shape of the trip changes.
With one week, you usually end up rushing
Cairo
and
Luxor
together, or Cairo and a Nile cruise. With ten days, the trip stays narrowly focused. With fourteen, you can see Cairo,
Giza
Aswan
, Luxor, and the temples along the Nile without having to push each into a single afternoon.
Two weeks is not unlimited.

Egypt is larger on the ground than it looks on a map. Cairo to Aswan is about 900 kilometres by air. Between Luxor and Aswan alone, the route is a continuous run of temples, river, villages, and desert cliffs. Once you try to add the Sinai, the Western Desert, the Red Sea, or
Alexandria
as well, two weeks quickly becomes a string of transfers.
A good two-week trip is built on what you choose not to add, more than on what you add.
What two weeks should be built around
For a first trip to Egypt, the natural shape is three centres.
First, Cairo and Giza. This is where you find the modern capital, the Islamic city, the Coptic quarter, the museums, and the Old Kingdom pyramids.
Second, Aswan. A southern town where the Nile is quieter, Nubian culture is close, and the gateway opens to Philae, the High Dam, and
Abu Simbel
Third, Luxor. The east and west banks of ancient Thebes — Karnak,
Luxor Temple
, the
Valley of the Kings
, the Hatshepsut mortuary temple, and
Medinet Habu

Three centres keep the trip from scattering. Cairo for the city and the museums. Aswan for the southern Nile. Luxor for New Kingdom kingship and the world of the dead. With Giza placed at the end, the pyramids stop being a famous picture and become something closer to the beginning of everything.
Why move from south to north
A lot of good two-week routes land in Cairo, fly south to Aswan early in the trip, and then move north toward Luxor.
There is a reason for that order.
The trip from Aswan to Luxor follows the flow of the Nile. It begins at Philae and moves through
Kom Ombo
Edfu

, and toward Luxor — and the temples themselves gradually become larger and more complex. Edfu is one of the best-preserved Ptolemaic temples; it makes the working logic of an Egyptian temple very legible. Kom Ombo has its unusual double dedication to two gods, with the architecture mirroring the theology. When you then arrive at Karnak, the enormous religious complex is easier to read not as sheer size but as long accumulation.
The other reason is Giza.

A lot of people land and want to go straight to the pyramids. That is not wrong. But putting Giza into the second half of the trip changes what it feels like. After you have seen the temples of Luxor and the Valley of the Kings, standing at Khufu's pyramid and knowing it is more than a thousand years older than any of them turns the time distance into something physical.
Closing the trip at Giza is, surprisingly, a strong piece of design.
A base two-week itinerary
Day 1: Arrive in Cairo
Don't load the first day with sites.

From Cairo International Airport, getting into the city takes anywhere from thirty minutes to over an hour depending on traffic. Check in, eat somewhere nearby, and use the rest of the day to let the body learn the rhythm of the city. Cairo is large and dense; going at full speed on the first day leaves fatigue running through the rest of the trip.
Day 2: Read Cairo in layers
The second day is for seeing Cairo not as one period but as a stacked city.

In the morning, head for the Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square. After the Grand Egyptian Museum opened, the main Tutankhamun destination moved to the GEM at Giza. The old Tahrir museum still carries the history of the building itself, the density of its older galleries, the Amarna material, and the memory of a long display tradition that supported the study of ancient Egypt for generations.
In the afternoon, the Islamic quarter. Walking around al-Azhar,
Khan el-Khalili
, al-Muizz Street, and a part of the Citadel makes clear that Egypt is not only an ancient country. The key here is not trying to do all of it. Cairo is not a city you can digest in half a day.
Day 3: Fly to Aswan
From Cairo to Aswan is about a 90-minute flight.
Aswan moves at a completely different speed from Cairo. The Nile is wider, granite outcrops break the water, and the air is dry in the way of the south.

In the afternoon, Philae is the natural priority. The temple of Isis was threatened with flooding after the construction of the old Aswan dam and was moved to its present location on Agilkia Island. The boat approach to the island is one of the more memorable temple arrivals in Egypt.
If time allows, add the High Dam as well. It is less a beauty spot than a way to read how modern Egypt has dealt with the Nile.
Day 4: Abu Simbel, or Aswan in depth
With two weeks, there is room for Abu Simbel.

The Great Temple of Ramses II and the small temple of Nefertari are south of Aswan, near Lake Nasser. The drive is long, with an early start. Even so, the colossal cut-rock façade and the story of the international rescue that lifted the temples to higher ground in the 1960s make it one of the strongest single days in any Egypt trip.
If Abu Simbel is not on the schedule, an alternative is to keep the day in Aswan for breathing room.
The Nubian Museum
Elephantine Island
, a felucca sail, the local markets. Aswan is not only a temple town. It is also a town for being on the water.
Days 5 to 7: North along the Nile
From Aswan to Luxor, there are several ways to travel: cruise, dahabiya, road, or train.
For a first trip, the easiest to read is a Nile cruise from Aswan to Luxor. The ship stops at Kom Ombo and Edfu on the way north, with the river running past the windows.
The temple at Kom Ombo, dedicated to Sobek and Horus, has a double structure. It stands facing the Nile, and the architectural symmetry literally builds the difference in theology into the stone.
The Temple of Horus at Edfu

is one of the best-preserved large temples in Egypt. Moving from the outer pylon through the court, the hypostyle hall, and the sanctuary, you can read how an Egyptian temple grows more sacred as it goes deeper.

The movement itself matters in this stretch. Fields, villages, palm groves, and desert cliffs line the bank. The mornings and evenings on the boat are not just a rest. They are the part of the trip where you understand the geography of Egypt in your body.
Day 8: Luxor east bank
When you arrive in Luxor, start on the east bank.

If you can, go to Karnak early. It is one of the largest religious complexes in the world, built and rebuilt from the Middle Kingdom through the Ptolemaic period. The Great Hypostyle Hall alone is overwhelming, but the real value of Karnak is not its scale. It is a place where the Amun priesthood, kingship, festival, and the memory of earlier kings have been layered on top of each other.

In the afternoon or evening, Luxor Temple. It stands inside the modern town and reads well under the night lighting. Karnak and Luxor Temple were once linked by an avenue of sphinxes. Seeing them not as separate sites but as parts of one festival map deepens both.
Day 9: Luxor west bank
The west bank is the world of the dead in ancient Thebes.

In the Valley of the Kings, the standard ticket lets you enter several of the open tombs. There are additional-ticket tombs as well, and the tomb of Seti I (KV17) is a strong choice if the budget and time allow. Tutankhamun's tomb is small and only modestly decorated, but it carries the weight of the story. If you plan to see the Tutankhamun treasures at the GEM, opinions are divided on whether the tomb itself is essential.

After that, the mortuary temple of Hatshepsut. The three terraces rising into the cliff face are a form unlike anything else in Egyptian architecture. Finish with the Colossi of Memnon, where you can begin to imagine the scale of the much larger mortuary temple of Amenhotep III that once stood behind them.

If there is time, Medinet Habu is worth adding. The mortuary temple of Ramses III preserves well-kept reliefs and surviving colour. If you must do the west bank in a single day, decide in advance what to include and what to leave out.
Day 10: Keep Luxor open
It is a waste to leave Luxor in a day and a half on a two-week trip.
Day 10 works well as a buffer. The Luxor Museum, the Mummification Museum, Medinet Habu, Deir el-Medina, the Ramesseum, or a second visit to Karnak — each choice changes the character of the trip.

This margin matters. Egyptian sites carry enormous information density, and if you push every day at full effort, by the second half everything starts to look like the same stone. Holding one day open in Luxor is a practical decision about the quality of the whole trip.
Day 11: Back to Cairo
From Luxor back to Cairo, the flight is short. The overnight sleeper train is an option as well; comfort levels are individual.
Don't pack the return day with heavy sightseeing. Check into a Cairo hotel and treat it as preparation for the GEM and Giza in the days ahead.
Day 12: The Grand Egyptian Museum

The Grand Egyptian Museum opened formally on 1 November 2025 and opened to the general public on 4 November, and it has changed how Cairo time gets spent. The complete Tutankhamun collection and Khufu's solar boat can now both be seen out near the Giza plateau.

The GEM is not a place to skim. Just the Tutankhamun galleries take real time to do properly. You can pair it with the pyramids on the same day, but going in depth means putting it on a different day.
Seeing the ancient Egyptian objects here and then going to Giza gives the pyramid visit a context the next day.
Day 13: Giza and Saqqara
Put Giza late in the trip.

The pyramids of Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure, the Great Sphinx, the surrounding cemeteries. Giza is a place you already know from photographs, and yet it is completely different to stand in. After Luxor and Aswan, it becomes easier to see how much older Old Kingdom architecture is, and how much it belongs to a different world.
If time and energy hold, add Saqqara. Djoser's step pyramid is a turning point in monumental stone architecture. Seeing Saqqara before or after Giza shows how royal tombs developed.
To pack Giza and Saqqara into a single day, you have to start early. If you plan to go inside the Great Pyramid, you also need to manage a separate ticket and time slot.
Day 14: Departure
The last day is built around the airport transfer.
Cairo traffic is hard to predict, and depending on the flight time it can be safer not to add morning sightseeing. If you do have margin, hold it to a short walk or a little shopping nearby.
A second two-week shape: the middle Nile
For a first trip to Egypt, the base itinerary above is the strongest option.

For a second-time visitor, or for someone with an interest in the Middle Kingdom, the Amarna period, or Coptic heritage, there is a different version that adds the middle Nile between Luxor and Cairo.

Around Minya you find Akhenaten's city at Amarna and the rock-cut tombs of Beni Hassan. Amarna is the surviving trace of one of the most unusual religious experiments in Egyptian history. The Beni Hassan tombs show the daily life of provincial officials — hunting, wrestling, craftwork — a living world quite different from the royal tombs.
Around Sohag are the White Monastery and the Red Monastery, both essential not only for ancient Egypt but for understanding the country's early Christian period.
Toward Fayoum are Meidum and Hawara, with their own pyramid stories distinct from Giza. Hawara is in particular connected with the funerary complex that ancient writers called "the Labyrinth."

This route is not for everyone. The travel load is heavier and the tourism infrastructure is thinner than in Cairo, Luxor, or Aswan. It suits second trips and more specialised interests, not first visits.
Season and fatigue
The most easily overlooked variable in a two-week Egypt trip is fatigue.

October through April is the easier travel season. December and January are crowded but the temperatures are comfortable. May through September is hot — in Luxor and Aswan you'll see days above 40°C. Summer travel needs to be built around early-morning sites and midday rest.

Inter-city movement also drives the fatigue. Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan are best connected by domestic flights. The sleeper train has its own romance, but the time and comfort trade-off varies by traveller. A Nile cruise combines movement and stay, which makes it easier to leave margin in the schedule.
Every three or four days, build in a quiet morning or a half-day off. This is not a luxury. It is operational work to protect the focus of week two.
Where to use a guide
You don't need a guide for every site in Egypt.

But for the Valley of the Kings, Karnak, the GEM, and Giza, a good Egyptologist guide makes a real difference. A good guide does not just hand you dates and names — they give you the frame for reading what you are looking at.

What the wall paintings in the Valley of the Kings are showing. Why the Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak is structured the way it is. How the pyramid, the mortuary temple, the causeway, and the valley temple at Giza connect. These are things that are hard to put together just by looking on the ground.
You don't need to add a guide for every day of a two-week trip. But adding one at the important places changes the quality of the visit.
What two weeks gives you
A two-week trip to Egypt is not a trip that finishes the understanding of Egypt.
It is a trip where the understanding begins.

The density of Cairo. The river at Aswan. The temples of Luxor. The silence of the Valley of the Kings. The GEM galleries. The scale of the stone at Giza. Once you have seen these in order, it becomes clear that Egypt is not a single period, a single image, or a single famous site.
With two weeks, the better choice is not to chase everything but to read the larger lines of the country.
South to north. From temples to tombs. From museum to plateau. From the New Kingdom back into the Old.

If that is the order you walk it in, then on the last day, standing at Giza, the pyramids stop feeling like the endpoint of a trip. They start looking more like the first question in a much longer Egyptian story.

deck: Two weeks is enough to link Cairo, Giza, Aswan, Luxor, and the Nile valley without rushing them. A practical guide to what to include and what to leave out.
